associated_movie.film_scene_description: Anne visits the Sorbonne chapel while investigating the mysterious circumstances surrounding Juan's death.

simple_description: The private chapel of the Sorbonne University in Paris.
medium_description: A historic Parisian chapel completed in 1642 at the request of Cardinal Richelieu. It represents an important example of French Baroque architecture in the heart of the Latin Quarter.
detailed_description: The Chapelle de la Sorbonne is a masterpiece of French Baroque architecture, designed by the architect Jacques Lemercier and completed in 1642. It was commissioned by Cardinal Richelieu, whose remains still rest today in the mausoleum within the nave. The structure is distinguished by its elegant dome, which was one of the first of its kind to be built in Paris, and is one of the intellectual symbols of the city.

child.simple_description: A cool historic church located inside Paris's famous university!
child.medium_description: Built way back in 1642 for Cardinal Richelieu, this church has a giant dome that looks like a king's crown in the middle of the student district.
child.detailed_description: Imagine stepping into a university chapel built over 350 years ago! Designed by Jacques Lemercier in 1642, it holds the tomb of Cardinal Richelieu. Its high round dome was one of the very first built in Paris, making it look like a magical castle tower where scholars studied ancient secrets.

professional.simple_description: A monumental French Baroque ecclesiastical structure within the Sorbonne complex.
professional.medium_description: Designed by Jacques Lemercier and consecrated in 1642, the Sorbonne Chapel stands as a pivotal milestone of French Classical Baroque architectural style, commissioned by Cardinal Richelieu.
professional.detailed_description: The Chapelle de la Sorbonne (1635–1642) represents a stylistic synthesis of Roman Baroque influence and traditional French double-tiered classical facades. Architect Jacques Lemercier designed the hemispherical dome over a double-drum, setting an architectural precedent for Parisian monumental domes. Featured prominently in Jacques Rivette's 'Paris nous appartient' (1961), the location evokes the intellectual and existential paranoia characteristic of early French New Wave cinema.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The characters pass through Place Saint-Sulpice and by the historic church during their journey across Paris.

simple_description: A large and historic Catholic church in the Odéon district.
medium_description: The second largest church in Paris after Notre-Dame, with construction beginning in 1646. It is famous for its imposing twin-tower facade and the astronomical gnomon located inside.
detailed_description: The Église Saint-Sulpice is a vast religious building located in the 6th arrondissement of Paris, whose construction origins date back to 1646, although it took over a century and a half to complete. It is famous for its imposing asymmetrical facade designed by Jean-Nicolas Servandoni and for the magnificent frescoes by Eugène Delacroix. The church also houses an important astronomical meridian (the gnomon of Saint-Sulpice) and a monumental Cavaillé-Coll organ, among the finest in France.

child.simple_description: A huge church with giant towers and a secret solar clock inside!
child.medium_description: This giant church is almost as big as Notre-Dame! It has two tall towers that look slightly different from each other and a special brass line on the floor that uses sunlight to tell time.
child.detailed_description: Saint-Sulpice is like a treasure hunt building! It took over 100 years to build starting in 1646. Inside, there is a golden astronomical line on the floor called a gnomon that measures solstice days when sunlight hits it. It also features giant organ pipes that produce thunderous musical sounds and colorful wall paintings by artist Eugène Delacroix!

professional.simple_description: An expansive 17th-century church showcasing Neoclassical and Baroque architectural transitions.
professional.medium_description: Initiated in 1646, Saint-Sulpice is celebrated for Jean-Nicolas Servandoni's Neoclassical bi-tiered portico facade, Delacroix's late romantic murals, and its precision 18th-century astronomical gnomon.
professional.detailed_description: The Église Saint-Sulpice stands as an architectural nexus of French late Baroque and emerging Neoclassicism. Servandoni's 1732 facade design introduced a dramatic double-colonnaded loggia flanking asymmetrical towers. The interior houses late masterpieces by Eugène Delacroix in the Chapelle des Anges (1861), alongside an 18th-century meridian line engineered for astronomical calculations. In New Wave filmography, it serves as an urban anchor in Rivette's cinematic cartography.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: A scenic sequence on the pedestrian bridge overlooking the Seine, where the characters discuss art and their theatrical ambitions.

simple_description: A famous pedestrian bridge crossing the Seine.
medium_description: The Pont des Arts is a metal pedestrian bridge connecting the Institut de France to the Louvre Museum. Originally built in 1804, it is famous worldwide as a romantic and scenic location.
detailed_description: The Pont des Arts, or Passerelle des Arts, was the first metal bridge built in Paris, originally inaugurated in 1804 under Napoleon Bonaparte. After being damaged by bombings and river collisions, it was rebuilt in the 1980s retaining a similar appearance to the original. It majestically connects the right and left banks of the Seine between the Louvre and the Institut de France, and is known in popular culture as the 'bridge of love locks', an unmissable destination for photographers and lovers.

child.simple_description: A wooden and metal bridge for walkers crossing the Seine River!
child.medium_description: Built for pedestrians, this bridge gives you amazing views of boats on the river and connects the famous Louvre art museum to the opposite riverbank.
child.detailed_description: The Pont des Arts was the very first iron bridge in Paris, built way back in 1804 under Emperor Napoleon! Since no cars are allowed, kids and artists love to stroll across, paint pictures, watch tour boats pass underneath, and enjoy the magical scenery of Paris right in the middle of the river.

professional.simple_description: The historic 1804 metallic pedestrian bridge crossing the Seine.
professional.medium_description: Engineered under Napoleon Bonaparte as the first metallic bridge in Paris, connecting the Louvre Palace to the Institut de France across nine cast-iron arches.
professional.detailed_description: Inaugurated in 1804, the Pont des Arts pioneered metallic civil engineering in Paris, utilizing nine cast-iron arches designed by Louis-Alexandre de Cessart and Jacques Dillon. Reconstructed in 1981–1984 with six steel arches to facilitate river navigation while maintaining structural heritage, the bridge serves as a iconic visual axis in Nouvelle Vague cinema—notably in Rivette's 'Paris nous appartient'—symbolizing artistic ambition and philosophical wandering.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The protagonists meet at the café near Place de l'Étoile to debate theater, politics, and bohemian life.

simple_description: An iconic Parisian café located near the Arc de Triomphe.
medium_description: A historic venue strategically positioned at Place de l'Étoile. It was a favorite meeting place for intellectuals, artists, and protagonists of the French New Wave.
detailed_description: Café le Presbourg is one of the iconic addresses of Parisian social and cultural life, set in the elegant surroundings of the Arc de Triomphe and Champs-Élysées district. A place of transit and pause for intellectuals and filmmakers throughout the twentieth century, it embodies the classic style of a French brasserie. Its vibrant atmosphere and period architecture make it the perfect stage for the dynamics and discussions that historically animated the Parisian cinema world.

child.medium_description: Famous movie directors and storytellers used to sit at small round tables here to eat pastries and invent exciting movie scripts.
child.detailed_description: Located near the giant stone arch of the Arc de Triomphe, Café le Presbourg is a classic French restaurant with bright lights and comfortable chairs. For many years, filmmakers and actors met here to sip hot chocolate, discuss cinema ideas, and watch people walk along the world's most famous street!

professional.simple_description: A seminal mid-century café frequented by Nouvelle Vague intellectuals near Place de l'Étoile.
professional.medium_description: Positioned on Rue de Presbourg overlooking the Arc de Triomphe, this venue functioned as a social hub for Parisian cinematic and literary avant-gardes during the 1950s and 60s.
professional.detailed_description: Café le Presbourg represents the quintessential Parisian bistro space transformed into an intellectual salon. Located adjacent to the monumental Haussmannian star junction of Place Charles de Gaulle, its spatial geography served both as a sanctuary for aesthetic debate and an authentic backdrop for New Wave filmmakers like Jacques Rivette, capturing authentic conversational dynamics in mid-20th-century urban Paris.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: A famous scene where the protagonists walk along the Seine with Notre-Dame in the background.

simple_description: Historic Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité.
medium_description: Notre-Dame de Paris is a majestic cathedral completed in 1345, a masterpiece of Gothic architecture. It is known worldwide for its gargoyles, rose windows, and flying buttresses.
detailed_description: Notre-Dame de Paris is the spiritual and geographical heart of Paris, located on the Île de la Cité. Built over roughly two centuries and completed in 1345, it defined the canons of Gothic architecture with its pioneering introduction of flying buttresses and rib vaults. Its priceless artistic heritage includes sculptures, medieval stained glass windows, and sacred relics. Having survived revolutions and wars, it continues to be an immortal symbol of French culture and resilience.

child.medium_description: Built hundreds of years ago on an island in the middle of Paris, this medieval cathedral has stone monsters called gargoyles perched high up on its towers.
child.detailed_description: Notre-Dame de Paris was finished in 1345 after nearly 200 years of work! It stands on a island right in the Seine River. It has enormous round stained-glass rose windows that shine bright red and blue when the sun hits them, and funny stone creatures called gargoyles that drain rainwater off the roof!

professional.simple_description: The quintessential French Gothic cathedral complex on Île de la Cité.
professional.medium_description: Constructed between 1163 and 1345, Notre-Dame de Paris established early Gothic engineering innovations including pioneer flying buttresses, pointed rib vaulting, and monumental rose windows.
professional.detailed_description: Notre-Dame de Paris stands as the apex of French Gothic sacral architecture. Initiated under Bishop Maurice de Sully in 1163, the cathedral pioneered high Gothic structural solutions—notably external flying buttresses designed to stabilize thin, high-reaching clerestory walls filled with stained glass. In Jean-Luc Godard's 'À bout de souffle' (1960), its towering presence anchors the urban roaming of Michel Poiccard and Patricia along the Seine.

location_name: Hotel Les Rives de Notre Dame, quai St Michel, Paris

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Michel and Patricia stroll along the riverbanks near the bouquinistes with the Notre-Dame Cathedral in the background.

simple_description: A hotel in the heart of Paris, formerly known as the Hotel de Suede.
medium_description: The Quai Saint-Michel is a famous street running along the left bank of the Seine. It offers one of the most iconic views of the Notre-Dame Cathedral and hosts numerous antique book stalls.
detailed_description: The Quai Saint-Michel is a historic street on the riverfront of the Parisian Rive Gauche, whose current layout largely dates back to medieval urban works and subsequent adjustments. It offers a picturesque and uninterrupted panoramic view of the nearby Notre-Dame Cathedral and the Île de la Cité. The banks are populated by the traditional 'bouquinistes', the open-air booksellers that characterize the bohemian and literary soul of the capital, making this walk a true immersion into history.

child.detailed_description: Right outside this historic hotel along Quai Saint-Michel, you can walk past the famous 'bouquinistes'—friendly open-air booksellers who open big green metal boxes filled with old books, posters, and postcards right along the river edge!

professional.medium_description: Situated on Quai Saint-Michel facing the Île de la Cité, this urban site embodies the literary and cinematic ambience of the Left Bank, immortalized in Godard's 'À bout de souffle'.
professional.detailed_description: The Quai Saint-Michel location (formerly Hôtel de Suède) represents an integral cinematic site in Jean-Luc Godard's seminal film 'À bout de souffle' (1960). The surrounding embankment urbanism, lined with traditional 'bouquinistes' and 19th-century residential facades, frames the iconoclastic roaming of Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg along the Seine.

location_name: The entrances to the George V Métro station

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Patricia sells copies of the New York Herald Tribune on the Champs-Élysées near the George V metro entrance.

simple_description: The historic entrance of a famous Parisian metro station.
medium_description: Opened in 1900 on Line 1, this station is located under the Champs-Élysées. Its entrances are typical of the Parisian metropolitan style, offering direct access to the city's most famous avenue.
detailed_description: The George V metro station, inaugurated on August 13, 1900, is located in the heart of the 8th arrondissement of Paris, serving the bustling and luxurious Avenue des Champs-Élysées. Originally named 'Alma', it was renamed in 1920 in honor of the King of England, George V, for British support during the First World War. The entrances reflect the functional yet iconic aesthetics of Parisian public transport, emerging directly onto the wide sidewalks where high society and global tourism intertwine.

child.detailed_description: This famous metro stop opened over 120 years ago! Kids love taking the stairs down into the underground train tunnels that zip across the city underneath the grand Champs-Élysées avenue.

professional.simple_description: An early 20th-century Paris Métro Line 1 entrance on Avenue des Champs-Élysées.
professional.medium_description: Inaugurated in August 1900 during the Exposition Universelle era, George V station showcases Art Nouveau influence and street-level access to the prestigious 8th arrondissement commercial corridor.
professional.detailed_description: Inaugurated in 1900 as 'Alma' and renamed 'George V' in 1920, this Métro Line 1 station entrance represents functional urban infrastructure integrated into Haussmannian boulevard design. In Godard's 'À bout de souffle', the station area serves as a kinetic backdrop where Patricia (Jean Seberg) sells the New York Herald Tribune, capturing raw Parisian street rhythm.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Michel Poiccard drives and walks across the monumental square during his travels across Paris.

simple_description: The largest and most famous square in Paris.
medium_description: A majestic public square located at the end of the Champs-Élysées, completed in 1772. It is famous for the ancient Egyptian obelisk at its center and its turbulent past during the French Revolution.
detailed_description: Place de la Concorde is the largest and most monumental square in Paris, designed by architect Ange-Jacques Gabriel and originally conceived as Place Louis XV. It became one of the main stages of the French Revolution, where the beheadings of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were carried out. At its center stands the Luxor Obelisk, an Egyptian artifact over 3,000 years old donated to France in the 19th century. Concluding the Champs-Élysées, it offers spectacular perspectives of the Tuileries Gardens, the Arc de Triomphe, and the Seine.

child.simple_description: Paris's biggest square featuring a real 3,000-year-old Egyptian obelisk!
child.medium_description: This giant open space has two beautiful fountains with water-spouting statues and a tall stone needle from ancient Egypt standing in the middle.
child.detailed_description: Place de la Concorde is a huge square filled with history! In the very middle stands the Luxor Obelisk, a giant carved stone tower gifted from Egypt that is over 3,000 years old. Around it are big golden fountains with water splashing into giant basins!

professional.simple_description: The monumental 18th-century urban square linking the Tuileries to the Champs-Élysées.
professional.medium_description: Designed by Ange-Jacques Gabriel in 1755, this octagonal urban space integrates Classical monumentality, twin colonnaded palaces, Hittorff's 19th-century fountains, and the 3,300-year-old Luxor Obelisk.
professional.detailed_description: Place de la Concorde represents a masterwork of French Neoclassical urban planning. Designed in an octagonal spatial layout bounded by dry moats and statuary, it evolved from an absolute royal monument into a revolutionary execution site and ultimately a unified civic square under Louis-Philippe. The erection of the 23-meter Egyptian obelisk in 1836 and Jacques-Ignace Hittorff's monumental fountains established its iconic visual geometry, frequently utilized as a dynamic driving location in French New Wave cinema.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Michel Poiccard spends time and meets contacts at the classic Montparnasse café.

simple_description: A classic Parisian brasserie in the Montparnasse district.
medium_description: Opened in 1923, Le Select was one of the favorite literary cafés for American expatriates and artists. It still maintains its charming original 1920s decor intact.
detailed_description: Le Select is a famous Parisian café and brasserie located at 99 Boulevard du Montparnasse. In the 1920s and 30s, it became the headquarters of the so-called 'Lost Generation', frequently visited by prominent literary and artistic figures such as Ernest Hemingway, F. Scott Fitzgerald, and Pablo Picasso. Unlike other modernized venues, Le Select has proudly maintained the authentic atmosphere and original booths of the era, remaining an intact temple of the bohemian spirit.

child.medium_description: Opened in 1923, this restaurant still looks just like it did 100 years ago when famous painters and storytellers ate here.
child.detailed_description: Le Select is a warm café with glowing lights and leather booths. A long time ago, famous storytellers like Ernest Hemingway and painters like Pablo Picasso sat right here to write stories and paint pictures while drinking warm tea.

professional.simple_description: A historically preserved 1920s Montparnasse literary café and brasserie.
professional.medium_description: Established in 1923, Le Select served as a quintessential gathering space for the interwar bohemian 'Lost Generation' and later mid-century film directors, maintaining its original Art Deco interior.
professional.detailed_description: Le Select at 99 Boulevard du Montparnasse remains an authentic site of interwar literary and artistic culture. Frequented by Hemingway, Picasso, and Anaïs Nin, its spatial continuity—retaining original mosaic tiling, wood paneling, and counter layout—made it an authentic location choice for Nouvelle Vague filmmakers seeking to capture authentic Montparnasse bohemian life.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Michel is shot by police and he runs down rue Campagne-Première before collapsing and dying near the Raspail metro station while exchanging final words with Patricia.

simple_description: A Parisian metro station on lines 4 and 6.
medium_description: Opened in 1906, this metro station serves the Montparnasse area. It takes its name from the boulevard above, dedicated to the chemist and politician François-Vincent Raspail.
detailed_description: The Raspail metro station is an underground hub located in the 14th arrondissement of Paris, inaugurated in 1906. It serves lines 4 and 6 and is strategically positioned in the Montparnasse district. The internal architecture features the classic beveled white tiles of the historic metro network. It serves as a vital vein for city transit and access to the historic sites of the Rive Gauche.

child.medium_description: Opened in 1906, trains run through tunnels underneath Montparnasse, stopping at tiled platforms deep under the city.
child.detailed_description: Raspail metro station is like a secret underground train room! Built over 100 years ago, its walls are covered in shiny white curved tiles that look like small bathroom bricks, making the station glow when trains zoom by!

professional.simple_description: A historic CMP network Métro station serving lines 4 and 6 in Montparnasse.
professional.medium_description: Opened in 1906, Raspail station exemplifies classic early 20th-century Parisian subterranean transit design featuring white bevel-edged ceramic tilework.
professional.detailed_description: Inaugurated in 1906 as part of the Compagnie du chemin de fer métropolitain de Paris (CMP) expansion, Raspail station connects lines 4 and 6 beneath Boulevard Raspail. In cinematic history, the surrounding streetscape (Rue Campagne-Première) provides the climactic backdrop for Jean-Paul Belmondo's dramatic collapse in the final scene of Godard's 'À bout de souffle'.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The trio visits the picturesque river island along the Marne during a quiet escape from the city.

simple_description: A small and picturesque river island near Paris.
medium_description: Located on the Marne River, the Island of the Crows (Île des Corbeaux) is part of the municipality of Saint-Maurice. It is a strip of natural land appreciated for walks surrounded by greenery.
detailed_description: Île des Corbeaux is a quiet and small river islet located on the Marne River, falling within the administrative territory of the municipality of Saint-Maurice, not far from the Bois de Vincennes, on the outskirts of Paris. The name evokes rural and wild atmospheres in stark contrast to urban expansion. Over time, these river islands have attracted Parisians looking for nature, offering idyllic landscapes and enchanting paths far from the urban frenzy.

child.detailed_description: Île des Corbeaux is a miniature island floating in the river! Covered in leafy trees and grass, it feels like a secret jungle hideout where movie characters go to escape the busy city.

professional.simple_description: A fluvial islet on the Marne River in Saint-Maurice, east of Paris.

professional.detailed_description: Île des Corbeaux in Saint-Maurice represents the idyllic riparian landscape of the Marne River banks. Historically associated with 19th-century 'guinguettes' leisure culture and Impressionist outdoor painting, the site served as an evocative suburban filming location in Jean-Luc Godard's 'Bande à part' (1964), highlighting stylistic contrasts between melancholic nature and urban crime themes.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The characters drive past the monumental column at Place de la Bastille in their convertible.

simple_description: An imposing monument located in Place de la Bastille.
medium_description: The July Column is a commemorative monument erected in 1840 to honor the victims of the July Revolution of 1830. Surmounted by the 'Spirit of Freedom', it dominates the Bastille intersection.
detailed_description: The Colonne de Juillet is a monumental bronze commemorative pillar located in the center of the renowned Place de la Bastille in Paris. Built between 1835 and 1840 under the reign of Louis Philippe, it commemorates the 'Trois Glorieuses', or the three days of the July Revolution of 1830. Engraved with the names of the victims, it is crowned by the famous gilded sculpture of the 'Spirit of Freedom' (Génie de la Liberté) by Auguste Dumont, a symbol of the republican spirit in motion.

adult.medium_description: The July Column is a commemorative monument erected in 1840 to honor the victims of the July Revolution of 1830. Surmounted by the 'Spirit of Freedom', it dominates the Bastille intersection.
adult.detailed_description: The Colonne de Juillet is a monumental bronze commemorative pillar located in the center of the renowned Place de la Bastille in Paris. Built between 1835 and 1840 under the reign of Louis Philippe, it commemorates the 'Trois Glorieuses', or the three days of the July Revolution of 1830. Engraved with the names of the victims, it is crowned by the famous gilded sculpture of the 'Spirit of Freedom' (Génie de la Liberté) by Auguste Dumont, a symbol of the republican spirit in motion.

child.simple_description: A tall bronze column with a golden winged statue shining at the top!
child.medium_description: Standing right where the old Bastille fortress used to be, this tall pillar has a golden statue holding a torch up in the sky.
child.detailed_description: The July Column is a giant bronze tower standing over 50 meters tall! At the very top stands the 'Génie de la Liberté'—a shiny gold-plated angel-like figure holding a flaming torch high in the air!

professional.simple_description: A monumental 50-meter bronze commemorative column in Place de la Bastille.
professional.medium_description: Designed by Jean-Antoine Alavoine and Joseph-Louis Duc, inaugurated in 1840 to commemorate the 1830 July Revolution, topped by Auguste Dumont's gilded statue 'Génie de la Liberté'.
professional.detailed_description: The Colonne de Juillet (1835–1840) is an architectural centerpiece of Place de la Bastille. Constructed of 21 bronze drums resting on a white marble pedestal, the column houses a funerary vault beneath. Surmounted by Auguste Dumont's gilt bronze 'Génie de la Liberté', the monument symbolizes French revolutionary republicanism. In Godard's 'Bande à part', the column anchors dynamic driving sequences through historic Paris.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Franz buys Odile the book she reminds him of on the quai de Conti on the Left Bank of the Seine

simple_description: An iconic street running along the left bank of the Seine.
medium_description: The Quai de Conti is located in the 6th arrondissement of Paris and houses prestigious buildings such as the Institut de France and the Monnaie de Paris. It is a hub of cultural and academic life.
detailed_description: The Quai de Conti is a historic riverside promenade located on the Rive Gauche in the 6th arrondissement of Paris, with roots dating back to the development of the river embankments since 1313. It is a walk of great architectural value and is dominated by two imposing institutions: the monumental headquarters of the Institut de France, under whose dome the Académie Française meets, and the Monnaie de Paris (Paris Mint). The quai captures the essence of Parisian elegance and the preservation of its high culture.

child.medium_description: You can walk along the Seine River here, pass by old coin-making palaces, and see big green domes rising into the sky.
child.detailed_description: Quai de Conti is a riverfront walk that has existed since 1313! Standing right across from the water is the Institut de France with its shiny dome where wise scholars meet, and the Paris Mint where gold coins were made long ago!

professional.simple_description: A historic riverside embankment on the Rive Gauche housing monumental civic institutions.
professional.medium_description: Dating from 1313, Quai de Conti features major Baroque and Neoclassical landmarks including the Institut de France (Le Vau, 1662) and the Monnaie de Paris (Antoine, 1775).
professional.detailed_description: The Quai de Conti represents a landmark section of the UNESCO-listed Seine riverfront. Dominated by Louis Le Vau's Collège des Quatre-Nations (now Institut de France) with its iconic French Baroque dome and Jacques-Denis Antoine's Neoclassical Monnaie de Paris, the quai captures academic prestige. In Godard's 'Bande à part' (1964), it provides a romantic strolling location for Franz and Odile.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: A famous sequence where Arthur, Franz, and Odile run through the Louvre galleries trying to beat the world record for visiting the museum.

simple_description: The most famous and largest art museum in the world.
medium_description: Initially conceived as a fortress and later as a royal palace, the Louvre opened as a museum in 1793. It houses priceless masterpieces such as Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa.
detailed_description: The Louvre Museum is the largest art museum exhibition in the world, nestled in the heart of Paris along the right bank of the Seine. Originally a medieval fortress in the 12th century, it was transformed into the main residence of the French kings, before becoming a public museum in 1793 during the French Revolution. Its countless galleries cover millennia of history and civilization, and its modern glass Pyramid now creates an extraordinary contrast between classical and contemporary architecture.

child.simple_description: A giant castle turned into the world's biggest art museum with a glass pyramid!
child.medium_description: Once a castle where kings lived, it is now filled with thousands of famous paintings like the Mona Lisa and famous statues!
child.detailed_description: The Louvre started as a medieval castle with moats 800 years ago, then became a royal palace for kings, and finally the world's greatest museum! It is so big that running through all its halls would take days!

professional.simple_description: The world's largest art museum and historic royal palace complex.
professional.medium_description: Evolving from a 12th-century Philip II fortress into a royal residence and opening as a national public museum in 1793, holding over 35,000 works of art.
professional.detailed_description: The Palais du Louvre embodies eight centuries of French architectural development—from Philippe Auguste's medieval fortress through Pierre Lescot's Renaissance facade and IM Pei's modern glass Pyramid (1989). In Jean-Luc Godard's 'Bande à part' (1964), the protagonists famously sprint through its classical galleries in 9 minutes and 43 seconds, executing an iconic irreverent gesture toward institutional high culture.

location_name: street market in Pl. de Levis

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The young narrator frequents the bustling market street of Place de Lévis while pursuing the bakery girl.

simple_description: A lively and historic neighborhood market in Paris.
medium_description: Located in the 17th arrondissement, the market around Place de Lévis is a popular pedestrian street known for its gastronomic excellence, offering cheese, wine, and fresh produce.
detailed_description: The street market that winds around Place de Lévis, in the 17th arrondissement of Paris, is one of the city's most beloved commercial and culinary promenades. Having transformed from a simple rural road in the 19th century into a modern pedestrian zone, the street retains the vibrant atmosphere of the classic Parisian 'marché de quartier' (neighborhood market). Visitors flock there for the abundance of artisan shops, fromageries, boulangeries, and stalls of prime produce, which fully represent the French art of living.

child.simple_description: A colorful outdoor food street market with freshly baked breads and fruits!
child.medium_description: Bakeries, fruit stalls, and cheese shops line this cozy pedestrian street where people shop every day for tasty snacks.
child.detailed_description: Place de Lévis is a bustling market street filled with delicious smells! You can see colorful fruit stands, bakeries selling warm crispy baguettes, and sweet pastry shops where Paris families get their daily treats!

professional.simple_description: A traditional 19th-century commercial street market in the 17th arrondissement.
professional.medium_description: The Rue de Lévis market represents an authentic Parisian permanent open-air food market, preserving neighborhood artisan food traditions and pedestrian urban life.
professional.detailed_description: The Place de Lévis food market exemplifies the traditional Parisian 'rue commerçante'. Transforming from an early 19th-century suburban village road into a dense pedestrian market street, it features specialized artisan food merchants. In Éric Rohmer's 'La Boulangère de Monceau' (1962), its daily pedestrian rhythms frame the protagonist's obsessive romantic surveillance.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine Doinel and René explore the lively Grands Boulevards near the cinema and covered passages.

simple_description: An address located along the famous Grands Boulevards of Paris.
medium_description: Located on the famous Boulevard Montmartre, in the vibrant heart of Paris, this address is close to the famous Passage Jouffroy. The area is historically known for its theaters and cafés.
detailed_description: The address at number 12 Boulevard Montmartre is part of the string of 'Grands Boulevards' in Paris, arteries born from the demolition of the old city walls. The 19th century saw this boulevard flourish as a center of high society and theatrical entertainment. In the immediate vicinity of number 12 are the entrances to the evocative Parisian covered passages, such as Passage Jouffroy, veritable arcades that enclose the soul of 19th-century French commerce.

child.simple_description: A busy boulevard full of cinemas, lights, and secret glass-roofed shopping alleys!
child.medium_description: Located on a grand street built long ago, right next to cool covered glass arcades filled with toy stores and vintage clocks.
child.detailed_description: Number 12 Boulevard Montmartre sits right on one of Paris's grandest streets! Right nearby is Passage Jouffroy—a magical covered shopping alley built with glass and iron roofs where kid movie characters explored in classic films!

professional.simple_description: A prime location on the 19th-century Grands Boulevards adjacent to Passage Jouffroy.
professional.medium_description: Boulevard Montmartre formed part of the historic 17th–19th century boulevard network, famous for entertainment, wax museums, and glass-covered arcades.
professional.detailed_description: Number 12 Boulevard Montmartre is situated on the boulevard urban network laid out on Louis XIV's former fortifications. Surrounding number 12 is the entrance to Passage Jouffroy (1845), a landmark metal-and-glass shopping arcade. In François Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups' (1959), Antoine Doinel and René roam these vibrant boulevards, capturing youthful freedom.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine wanders through the secluded Montmartre street running alongside the cemetery wall.

simple_description: A small street nestled in the Montmartre district.
medium_description: Located in the artistic 18th arrondissement, Rue Puget is a short street that reflects the classic bohemian charm of the Montmartre hill, adjacent to the famous eponymous cemetery.
detailed_description: Number 2 Rue Puget is situated on a quiet, short street in the 18th arrondissement of Paris, right in the atmosphere of Montmartre. The street runs tightly against the protective walls of the famous Montmartre Cemetery, where countless French intellectual figures rest. Despite its secluded position away from the main tourist routes, the surrounding architecture perfectly reflects the residential character and the romantic, slightly decadent appearance typical of the Belle Époque.

child.medium_description: A peaceful street running along an old stone wall, far away from big noisy traffic.
child.detailed_description: Rue Puget is a quiet little road near the famous Montmartre hill! It has cozy apartment buildings with metal balconies where cats sleep in the sun, perfect for kids playing secret adventure games!

professional.simple_description: A secluded residential street adjacent to the Montmartre Cemetery in the 18th arrondissement.
professional.medium_description: Rue Puget represents typical late 19th-century Parisian residential urbanism running alongside the perimeter wall of the Montmartre Cemetery.
professional.detailed_description: Located at 2 Rue Puget in the 18th arrondissement, this brief street alignment illustrates the quiet residential fabric of lower Montmartre. Bordering the stone wall of the Cimetière de Montmartre, its atmosphere was captured by François Truffaut in 'Les 400 coups' (1959) to evoke Antoine Doinel's urban isolation and wandering.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine walks up the iconic winding street in the heart of Montmartre.

simple_description: A historic address on the famous winding street of Montmartre.
medium_description: At the beginning of Rue Lepic, a short walk from the Moulin Rouge, this address paves the way to the top of Montmartre. The street is known for its historic cafés and for having hosted great artists.
detailed_description: Number 3 Rue Lepic marks the beginning of one of the most iconic and ancient streets in the Montmartre district, originally traced out in 1852 by Emperor Napoleon III to facilitate the ascent up the hill. Starting from Boulevard de Clichy, the address introduces pedestrians to the lively uphill path. Giants of art such as Vincent van Gogh have lived along Rue Lepic, making the entire artery a true open-air scenography, perfect for cinema.

child.medium_description: Starting right near the Moulin Rouge windmill, this winding street leads up the hill past bakeries and art studios.
child.detailed_description: Rue Lepic winds all the way up the Montmartre hill! Famous painters like Vincent van Gogh walked up these same cobblestones over 100 years ago carrying paintbrushes and canvases!

professional.simple_description: The lower origin of Rue Lepic, a historic arterial street climbing the Montmartre hill.
professional.medium_description: Traced in 1852 to replace steep village tracks, Rue Lepic winds past historic windmills, artists' residences (Van Gogh at No. 54), and local market shops.
professional.detailed_description: Number 3 Rue Lepic sits at the junction with Boulevard de Clichy. Designed under Napoleon III in 1852 as Chemin de Ronde d'Epinettes, Rue Lepic curves gently up the Butte Montmartre. Retaining its historic artisan storefronts and urban charm, it served as a key location shot in Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups'.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine and René play near the fountains and gardens of the square facing the Sainte-Trinité church.

simple_description: A scenic square in front of the Trinité Church.
medium_description: Formerly known as Square de la Trinité, it is a green space designed by architect Adolphe Alphand. It offers a magnificent perspective of the imposing Église de la Sainte-Trinité.
detailed_description: The Square d'Estienne d'Orves is a charming tree-lined square located in the 9th arrondissement of Paris. It was created in 1866 as part of the great Haussmannian works to serve as an elegant frame for the adjacent Church of the Sainte-Trinité. Later renowned to honor the name of a hero of the French Resistance, the square is a refined urban hub featuring allegorical fountains surrounded by carefully modeled flower beds.

child.medium_description: A green park with trees, benches, and fountains where birds splash, directly facing a grand church tower.
child.detailed_description: Square d'Estienne d'Orves is a green garden square created in 1866! It has three fountain basins with water spraying into the air, big shade trees, and gravel paths where kids and friends play in front of the huge Trinité church.

professional.simple_description: A Second Empire landscaped civic square framed by the Église de la Sainte-Trinité.
professional.medium_description: Designed in 1866 by Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand under Baron Haussmann, featuring allegorical fountains by Gabriel Davioud framing Théodore Ballu's Church of the Holy Trinity.
professional.detailed_description: Square d'Estienne d'Orves (formerly Square de la Trinité) represents Haussmannian civic landscape design. Conceived by Alphand to provide a monumental foreground perspective for Ballu's Église de la Sainte-Trinité (1861–1867), the square integrates Davioud's stone fountains and allegorical sculptures. Featured in Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups', it serves as a backdrop for juvenile freedom.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine roams the heights of Montmartre with the Sacré-Cœur basilica standing in the background.

simple_description: A magnificent white basilica at the top of the Montmartre hill.
medium_description: Built between the late 19th century and 1914, the Basilica of the Sacred Heart is the highest point in Paris. Its Romano-Byzantine architecture offers a spectacular view over the entire city.
detailed_description: The Sacré-Cœur Basilica is a grand Catholic place of worship that dominates the city from the summit of the Montmartre butte. Construction began in 1875 and the structure was completed in 1914. It is characterized by its luminous limestone, known for cleaning itself with rain, and by an eclectic style that combines Romanesque and Byzantine influences. From its monumental parvise, one can admire one of the most extraordinary and vast panoramas of the entire French capital.

child.simple_description: A shiny white cathedral at the very top of the highest hill in Paris!
child.medium_description: Looking like a giant white ice-cream castle, this church stays bright white even when it rains and lets you see the whole city of Paris below!
child.detailed_description: Sacré-Cœur stands on the highest hill in Paris! It is made from special white stones that wash themselves clean whenever rain falls. From the top stairs, you can look down and see the entire city stretched out like a giant toy map!

professional.simple_description: The hilltop Romano-Byzantine basilica crowning the Butte Montmartre.
professional.medium_description: Constructed 1875–1914 by Paul Abadie, built with self-cleaning Château-Landon travertine, representing an iconic architectural landmark at the city's highest elevation.
professional.detailed_description: The Basilique du Sacré-Cœur (1875–1914) commands the summit of Butte Montmartre (130m elevation). Designed by Paul Abadie in an eclectic Romano-Byzantine style featuring a monumental central dome and campana tower housing the 19-ton 'Savoyarde' bell. The building's travertine stone secretes calcite upon contact with rainwater, maintaining its bright white appearance. In Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups', its silhouette symbolizes Paris.

location_name: Champs Elysées (60 avenue des Champs Elysées)

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine and his friend steal a typewriter from an office located on the Champs-Élysées.

simple_description: An address on the most famous avenue in the world in Paris.
medium_description: At number 60 of the famous Avenue des Champs-Élysées, you are in the beating heart of Parisian luxury. The avenue extends from Place de la Concorde to the imposing Arc de Triomphe.
detailed_description: Number 60 Avenue des Champs-Élysées is located along the majestic perspective axis that defines the triumph of Parisian urban planning. Originally traced out by André Le Nôtre in 1670, the avenue took its final shape in the 18th century, becoming the symbol of national grandeur. Hosting haute couture boutiques, historic automobile showrooms, restaurants, and luxury cafés, this stretch of the avenue embodies the undisputed prestige of the city, lending itself to countless cinematic shots.

child.medium_description: A famous wide avenue where grand parades happen, lined with trees, cinemas, and sparkling store displays.
child.detailed_description: Number 60 Champs-Élysées sits on a super wide avenue built over 350 years ago! Thousands of people walk along its wide stone sidewalks every day to watch parades, visit shops, and see famous movie theaters!

professional.simple_description: A central address on the monumental Avenue des Champs-Élysées urban axis.
professional.medium_description: Traced by André Le Nôtre in 1670 and expanded in the 18th and 19th centuries into a 1.9 km grand avenue connecting Place de la Concorde to Arc de Triomphe.
professional.detailed_description: Located at 60 Avenue des Champs-Élysées in the 8th arrondissement, this site sits on the 'Axe historique' of Paris. Originally designed in 1670 by Le Nôtre as an extension of the Tuileries gardens, the avenue evolved into a symbol of French prestige and cinema commerce. In Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups', Antoine Doinel and René visit an office here during their typewriter theft adventure.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Antoine looks out over the Trocadéro esplanade with the iconic view of the Eiffel Tower.

simple_description: A large exhibition building with the best view of the Eiffel Tower.
medium_description: Built in Art Deco style for the 1937 Universal Exhibition, it is located on the Chaillot hill. Its famous esplanade offers a breathtaking panorama of the Trocadéro gardens.
detailed_description: The Palais de Chaillot is a majestic architectural complex located in the 16th arrondissement, at the peak of the Chaillot hill. It was built for the 1937 International Exhibition. Composed of two large curved wings separated by a monumental esplanade, it offers by far the most famous and emblematic framing of the Eiffel Tower on the other bank of the Seine. It houses prestigious museums inside, such as the Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine.

child.simple_description: A grand Art Deco palace with the coolest view of the Eiffel Tower!
child.medium_description: Two big curved buildings facing a giant stone terrace where you can stand and take amazing photos right across from the Eiffel Tower!
child.detailed_description: Built in 1937, the Palais de Chaillot has two big curving wings and a wide stone terrace. When you stand in the middle, the Eiffel Tower looks so close you feel like you could reach out and touch it!

professional.simple_description: The monumental 1937 Art Deco architectural complex at Trocadéro.
professional.medium_description: Designed by Louis-Auguste Boileau, Jacques Carlu, and Léon Azéma for the 1937 Exposition Internationale, featuring two curved pavilion wings framing the iconic Eiffel Tower perspective.
professional.detailed_description: The Palais de Chaillot (1937) replaced the 1878 Moorish Trocadéro Palace on the Chaillot hill. Designed in classical Art Deco monumentality, its twin curving wings are separated by the Parvis des Droits de l'Homme, offering the canonical urban framing of the Eiffel Tower and Champ de Mars. A iconic visual setting in Truffaut's 'Les 400 coups' and French cinema history.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: Cléo walks along the historic arcades of Rue de Rivoli after visiting the fortune teller.

simple_description: An address along one of the main shopping streets in Paris.
medium_description: Located along the famous commercial arcades, Rue de Rivoli was founded by Napoleon Bonaparte. This address is very close to central monuments, including the Louvre.
detailed_description: Number 128 Rue de Rivoli is part of one of the longest, most central, and most historic arteries in the city of Paris. The street was designed and initiated in 1802 with the characteristic structure of uniform arcades and colonnades alongside the Tuileries Gardens and the Louvre. This commercial stretch connects the city's main monumental axes and reflects the splendor of the imperial era through the unmistakable alignment of its imposing stone facades.

child.simple_description: A famous street lined with stone arches where you can walk out of the rain!
child.medium_description: Built over 200 years ago under Napoleon, this street has long covered archways filled with shops right next to the Louvre.
child.detailed_description: Rue de Rivoli has covered stone arches built over 200 years ago so people could go shopping without ever getting wet in the rain! It runs straight through the middle of Paris right past the Louvre Museum.

professional.simple_description: A central arcaded street address constructed under Napoleon Bonaparte.
professional.medium_description: Commissioned in 1802 by Napoleon I and designed by Percier and Fontaine, featuring unified Neoclassical arcaded facades along the Tuileries Gardens.
professional.detailed_description: Number 128 Rue de Rivoli represents early 19th-century French urban rationalism. Designed by Charles Percier and Pierre-François-Léonard Fontaine, the street established strict architectural uniformity with continuous stone arcades. In Agnès Varda's 'Cléo de 5 à 7' (1962), Cléo walks along these arcades in real-time cinematic narrative.

simple_description: A historic intellectual café in the Montparnasse district.
medium_description: Opened in 1898, Le Dôme was the first true gathering place for intellectuals in Montparnasse. Artists and writers who frequented it were nicknamed 'Dômiers'.
detailed_description: The Café du Dôme is a true Parisian cultural institution inaugurated in 1898 at the corner of Boulevard du Montparnasse and Boulevard Raspail. At the beginning of the 20th century, it became the nerve center of intellectual life on the Rive Gauche, attracting prominent international painters, sculptors, poets, and writers of the Anglo-American and Eastern European scenes. Today, it still perfectly preserves its status as a legend of the golden age of French bohemian and cinematic art.

simple_description: A large and peaceful English-style public park in the south of Paris.
medium_description: Designed by Adolphe Alphand at the request of Napoleon III in 1869, Parc Montsouris covers 15 hectares. It is known for its large artificial lake, waterfalls, and rich vegetation.
detailed_description: Parc Montsouris is one of the four large urban parks commissioned by Emperor Napoleon III to offer green oxygen zones to the capital, officially opened in 1869. Located in the 14th arrondissement near the Cité Universitaire, it was designed by the brilliant engineer Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand in a typical English landscape style, transforming an area of abandoned quarries. It is dominated by a vast central artificial lake that makes it a serene oasis as much appreciated by students as by filmmakers.

professional.simple_description: A 15-hectare Second Empire English landscape park in the 14th arrondissement.
professional.medium_description: Engineered by Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand and opened in 1869 under Napoleon III, featuring an artificial lake, cascading waterfalls, and diverse botanical flora.
professional.detailed_description: Parc Montsouris (1869) represents the zenith of Second Empire urban park creation engineered by Alphand. Built over former subterranean quarries and railway tracks, the 15-hectare park features an artificial lake, weeping willows, and winding contours. In Agnès Varda's 'Cléo de 5 à 7' (1962), the park serves as a serene backdrop where Cléo meets Antoine.

associated_movie.film_scene_description: The opening sequences feature the bustling traffic and views around the monumental arch at Place de l'Étoile.

simple_description: An iconic monumental arch standing at the western end of the Champs-Élysées.
medium_description: Commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 to honor French military victories, this Neoclassical monument stands at the center of Place de l'Étoile. It shelters the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and serves as the monumental anchor of Paris's historic axis.
detailed_description: The Arc de Triomphe is one of the most celebrated monuments in France, commissioned by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1806 following the victory at Austerlitz and inaugurated in 1836 under King Louis-Philippe. Designed in a monumental Neoclassical style by architect Jean Chalgrin, it commands the center of Place Charles de Gaulle (historically Place de l'Étoile), from which twelve grand avenues radiate outwards. The structure is renowned for its high-relief sculptural groups, notably François Rude's 'La Marseillaise', celebrating the French Revolutionary and Imperial campaigns. Beneath its arch lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and the eternal flame rekindled daily since 1923, making it both a primary site of national remembrance and a defining visual landmark of Parisian cinema.

child.detailed_description: The Arc de Triomphe is a massive stone arch that stands 50 meters tall! Emperor Napoleon ordered it built in 1806. Twelve wide avenues meet around it forming a big star shape, and at night an eternal flame glows under the arch!

professional.simple_description: The iconic 1806 Neoclassical triumphal arch anchoring the Place Charles de Gaulle star junction.
professional.medium_description: Commissioned by Napoleon I in 1806 and inaugurated in 1836, designed by Jean Chalgrin, featuring François Rude's masterwork relief 'La Marseillaise'.
professional.detailed_description: The Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile (1806–1836) stands as a monument of French Neoclassical architecture. Designed by Jean Chalgrin and completed under Louis-Philippe, its 50-meter colossus features monumental relief sculptures, notably François Rude's 'Le Départ des Volontaires de 1792' (La Marseillaise). Positioned at the apex of the twelve radiating avenues of Place Charles de Gaulle, it serves as an urban anchor in Rivette's 'Paris nous appartient' (1961).
